title: High Rank Is Won with Keen and Cutting Swords
intro: Ibn al-Muqarrab wrote this for the amir Muhammad ibn Abi al-Husayn of the Uyunid house in 599 AH (1202–3 CE), when the amir took al-Ahsa; the heading in the diwan calls it his first poem after two earlier ones whose copies he lost. It opens with a maxim, that high rank is won with swords, spears and horses, not with songs and lovers, and makes the amir the man from whom such glory is learned. Then it tells of his campaigns, against the Banu Malik of Tayyi', against Ghaziyya and al-Muntafiq, and against the Arabs of Syria who marched on Bahrain, and ends with the caliph's favour and a prayer for the amir. Some manuscripts add that when the amir asked what he wanted in return, the poet said he needed nothing: “it is something that came into my heart, and I found you worthy of it.” The old commentary printed with the diwan tells the story of each battle, and the editor, Abd al-Khaliq al-Janbi, notes that the historians of Iraq left the Syrian campaign out.

translation: High rank is won with keen and cutting swords,
with tawny spears and lean, well-bred horses.
1.sharh: Glory is won only by war: by keen swords, long spears and lean, well-bred horses. The maxim opens the poem and prepares its praise of the amir, who won his rank by just these means.

translation: And with thrusts when the dust is up, and the sons
of war come on like stallion camels never broken,
2.sharh: Glory also takes spear-thrusts in the thick of battle, when the dust flies and seasoned warriors charge like stallion camels no one has broken. The courage he means is courage against men like these.

translation: and with blows that strike the heads from every noble man,
bold in the face of terror, of high descent.
3.sharh: Glory takes sword-blows too, the kind that strike off the heads of brave men of good family. A victory is worth as much as the enemy, and these are noble, fearless men, not weaklings.

translation: Glory is not won by one whose care
is the modes of song, or the embrace of lovers.
4.sharh: No one wins glory whose mind is on music and lovers' embraces. The line sets a life of pleasure against the life of war described before it.

translation: None has reached the heights but a free woman's son
who gives little thought to how things may end.
5.sharh: Only a man of free and noble birth reaches the heights, one who acts without dwelling on what may follow. The old commentator notes that the Arabs praised such disregard for consequences, though the wise condemned it.

translation: Bold against his foes, and bitter to their taste,
far in his aims, rich in bounty and in gifts.
6.sharh: He is bold against his enemies and bitter to them, aims far, and gives freely. Harshness to foes and generosity to everyone else are the two halves of the ideal chief.

translation: Sworn friend of night journeys, a ranger of lands; his camels
have carried him across the heart of empty, endless wastes.
7.sharh: He is never parted from night travel, as if sworn to it, and his camels have carried him through the heart of empty deserts. Restless hardship is part of the hero's portrait.

translation: Horses have waded with him through blood, and his spears
have snapped by force in the chests of the battalions.
8.sharh: His horse has waded through blood with him, and his spears have snapped in the front ranks of the enemy. A spear broken in the enemy is the sign of a thrust driven home.

translation: He learned from the deeds of the amir Muhammad,
and so became a king in the loftiest of ranks.
9.sharh: Such a man learned his ways from the deeds of the amir Muhammad, and they raised him to kingship. The amir is made the teacher of glory, and with his name the poem turns from maxims to praise.

translation: A young man whose horses, every single day,
share out the riches of the warring enemy.
10.sharh: Not a day passes without his horses bringing in the enemy's goods to be shared out as spoils. The horses are said to do the sharing because they win the plunder.

translation: On them a noble, awe-inspiring man makes his raids,
quick to answer a grave call, far-reaching in his quests.
11.sharh: On those horses an awe-inspiring, noble man raids on every side, quick to answer any grave call. His gains lie far off, the old commentator explains, because he takes them from enemies abroad, not from his own subjects.

translation: A brave man: when the camp wakes to the morning,
its morning draught is nothing but keen-edged swords.
12.sharh: When a camp he raids wakes up, the only morning drink it gets is the edge of his swords. The verb for waking, asbaha, and sabuh, the morning draught, share a root, and the line turns the drink of a peaceful dawn into the sword.

translation: He drove the enemy from their guarded land and took it,
and their lions became like foxes before him.
13.sharh: He drove his enemies from the land they guarded and took it for himself, and their lions turned into foxes before him. The great among his foes, the commentator says, became small in the face of his might.

translation: No land is left that his horses have not crossed,
its mountains crushed beneath their mighty shoulders.
14.sharh: His horses have crossed every land and crushed its mountains under the force of their shoulders. Manakib can also mean the high ground, and some read the line as the land's corners broken along with its heights.

translation: Ask the sons of Malik what he is in war:
one who was there knows what no absent man knows.
15.sharh: Ask the Banu Malik what he is like in war; they were there, and a witness knows what no absent man can. He points to his rout of them instead of describing it.

translation: The morning they turned in flight and gave up,
against their will, every fair young maiden.
16.sharh: That was the morning they turned and fled, leaving behind, against their will, every fair young woman of the tribe. To abandon its women was the worst disgrace a tribe could suffer.

translation: He came on them with an army that filled the horizon,
young men and grey, with no care but glory.
17.sharh: He came at them with an army that filled the horizon, young men and grey-haired alike, all with no aim but glory. Old and young turning out together shows a whole people behind him.

translation: When they saw him and knew that it was he,
they had no weapon but the dust of the long-bodied horses.
18.sharh: Once they saw him and knew it was really he, they did not fight; their only weapon was the dust their horses kicked up as they fled. The commentator explains that they used the dust as if it were a weapon to shield them.

translation: Did Ghaziyya keep its home from him
with tawny, quivering spears and white, cutting blades?
19.sharh: Ghaziyya could not defend its home from him with spear or sword; the question expects the answer no. The next lines tell how they fell.

translation: The morning he came upon them in a sky of dust,
his spearheads under it like stars.
20.sharh: He came upon them under a sky of dust raised by his horses, with his spearheads glinting beneath it like stars. The image sets the gloom of the dust against the flash of steel.

translation: A warner had come to them from him, telling them to move
off the middle of the road to one side of the desert.
21.sharh: He had sent them a warning to move off his path to one side of the desert. According to the commentator he was after al-Muntafiq alone, who were camped with Ghaziyya, and he told Ghaziyya to stand apart.

translation: They would not take the well-wisher's counsel, and turned away,
and thought such thoughts, and how false they were.
22.sharh: Ghaziyya refused the warning, sure they could stand against him, and their confidence proved utterly false. The cry at the end of the line marks how badly they misjudged him.

translation: He fell on them at dawn with a far-flung raid that closed to them
the wide deserts, east and west.
23.sharh: He fell on them at dawn with a raid that spread out on every side and closed the open desert to them east and west, leaving nowhere to run.

translation: They stayed no longer than the pause between two milkings, then bolted
as sheep bolt from hungry wolves.
24.sharh: They held their ground for only a moment, then scattered like sheep before hungry wolves. The comparison makes them helpless flocks and his horsemen the wolves.

translation: They left their wealth behind in shame, and gave up
women of sweet mouths and laughing breasts.
25.sharh: They left their herds and goods behind in disgrace, and their women too. The women are named only by their beauty: sweet mouths and breasts so fair they seem to laugh.

translation: Ibn Madhkur flew off, whipping on his young camels
and warning every friend about his raids.
26.sharh: Ibn Madhkur fled as if on wings, driving his young camels hard and warning all his friends of the amir's raids. He saved himself by speed, not courage.

translation: He kept no faith with the pact he had with Dahmash,
and said, “In such a plight, no one is bound to keep his word.”
27.sharh: Ibn Madhkur broke his pact with Dahmash and his people and excused himself by saying that no one is bound to keep faith in such straits. Ghaziyya kept to the pact and bore most of the slaughter.

translation: And when the men of Syria came, with death
leading them to him as a spare horse is led to its rider,
28.sharh: When the Arabs of Syria came, death led them to him as a spare horse is led beside its rider, docile and unknowing. The sentence is completed in line 31: when they came, he rode out to meet them.

translation: Sa'id and Mas'ud and the clan of Hudaytha,
driving their sleek horses among swift camels,
29.sharh: The Syrian Arabs came under their own amirs and clans, driving fine horses among swift camels. The commentator says these amirs lived among Tayyi' and led that tribe.

translation: having mustered the men of the Hijaz, and come
out of Syria with their families and war bands,
30.sharh: They had raised the tribes of the Hijaz and come out of Syria with their families and war bands, meaning to take Bahrain. The commentator says they planned to strike first at Ubada, Khafaja and the other Uqayl clans in Iraq.

translation: he came at them across the wastes with horse and spear,
a young man of Abd Allah's line, fearless in battle.
31.sharh: Then the amir rode out to meet them across the deserts with horse and spear, a young man of Abd Allah's line who feared no battle. This line completes the sentence begun in line 28.

translation: Striker of champions' heads, used to holding
the rear in a chase, and to giving lavish gifts.
32.sharh: He strikes at the heads of armoured champions, and is used to guarding the rear of the horsemen in a chase and to giving lavish gifts. Holding the rear, where the danger lay, was the mark of the bravest rider.

translation: Nothing saved them but flight, and a protection
he gave them that no fault-finder could fault.
33.sharh: Only flight saved them, and then the protection he granted them, which no one could fault him for. The commentator says they sent to remind him that they too were of Rabi'a, his own stock, and he spared their lives, goods and women.

translation: They had claimed in their boasting that their horses
would trample the villages of Bahrain on every side.
34.sharh: The Syrians had boasted that their horses would trample the villages of Bahrain on every side. The next lines say what stood in their way.

translation: Far out of reach was what they tried, for in its way stood
the swords of Ibn Fadl, the man of rank and virtue,
35.sharh: What they hoped for was far beyond reach, with the swords of Ibn Fadl in the way. To reach the villages of Bahrain they would first have to get past those swords.

translation: and true young men of Uqayl, proud and mighty,
heavy on their foes, and of noble descent.
36.sharh: Also in their way stood the brave young men of Uqayl, proud and of noble descent, a heavy weight on their enemies. The commentator says these clans joined the amir against the Syrians.

translation: Through him they won their hopes and all their wishes,
and took the highest seats of eminence.
37.sharh: Through him they won all they hoped for and rose to the highest honour, since he turned back the army that meant to fall on them first.

translation: He is the fierce lion, and the lord
who built his glory above the shining stars.
38.sharh: He is a fierce lion in war and a lord whose glory is built higher than the brightest stars. Thawaqib, the word for the stars, means those that pierce the dark.

translation: The thick-necked bowed down to him, and through him
the land is radiant after those dark times.
39.sharh: The proudest men bowed their thick necks to him, and through him the land shone again after its dark times. The darkness is the troubled time before his reign, and his rule is the light that ended it.

translation: You see the envoys of kings stay on at his court:
one envoy leaves as another arrives,
40.sharh: Envoys of kings are always at his court; one leaves just as another arrives. The commentator says the kings kept him busy with embassies to show their goodwill.

translation: for fear of his assaults, which they know well,
and which raise the mourners' wailing over his foes,
41.sharh: They do so for fear of the assaults they know too well, which leave mourners wailing over the enemy's dead. The embassies are meant to keep those attacks away.

translation: assaults inherited from the days of Ad and Jurhum,
of Wuhayb ibn Afsa, and the generations gone.
42.sharh: Such assaults are no new thing in him: his house has inherited them since the days of Ad and Jurhum, of Wuhayb ibn Afsa and the vanished generations. The commentator says such might has been the custom of his house and tribe for as long as there have been Arabs.

translation: The Commander of the Faithful turned his favour
to him, and named him Chief of the Arabs.
43.sharh: The caliph favoured him with robes of honour and gifts and titled him Chief of the Arabs, as the commentator reports. The kings fear him, and the caliph holds him dear.

translation: He guarded the desert from the edge of Iraq and held it
to Syria, and took the land to the bounds of Na'ib.
44.sharh: He guarded the open desert from the borders of Iraq, held it all the way to Syria, and took the land as far as Na'ib in Oman. The line maps a realm reaching across Arabia.

translation: Under his lofty might all who were frightened
and afraid grew strong, and his bounty made all seekers rich.
45.sharh: Under the shelter of his might every frightened man found strength, and his generosity made every seeker rich. One manuscript has “found rest” for “grew strong”.

translation: May Rabi'a never for a day be without one like him
to build its glory or to give its gifts.
46.sharh: He prays that Rabi'a, the great tribe to which the amir and the poet both belong, may never lack a man like him to raise its glory and give its gifts.

translation: May his days never cease to pass in happiness,
and may he stay guarded, his domain and every side.
47.sharh: The poem closes with a prayer that his days stay happy and his realm stay guarded on every side. A man who raids in every direction has enemies in every direction, so the prayer fits the man the poem has drawn.

1.1.3.head: المُرهَفات
1.1.3.meaning: Murhafat: swords with thin, keen edges.

1.2.1-2.head: سُمر العَوالي
1.2.1-2.meaning: “Tawny heights”: spears, named for their brown shafts and their tips.

1.2.4.head: الشَّوازِب
1.2.4.meaning: Lean, hard-trained; a lean horse was ready for raiding.

2.2.5.head: المَصاعِب
2.2.5.meaning: Stallion camels never ridden or loaded, and so never tamed.

4.2.1-2.head: طُروق الأَغاني
4.2.1-2.meaning: Turuq al-aghani: the modes and tunes of song, as the commentator explains.

5.1.5-6.head: اِبن حُرَّة
5.1.5-6.meaning: “Son of a free woman”: a man of noble birth on both sides, not the son of a slave.

6.2.3-4.head: جَمّ النَّدى
6.2.3-4.meaning: “Abundant in dew”: lavishly generous; nada, dew, is a common word for generosity.

7.1.1-2.meaning: “Ally of night travel”: always travelling by night.

7.2.2.head: العيس
7.2.2.meaning: Is: pale camels, the prized riding camels.

9.1.5.meaning: Muhammad: the amir Muhammad ibn Abi al-Husayn of the Uyunid house, the poem's patron, who took al-Ahsa in 599 AH (1202–3 CE) and so ruled all of Bahrain.

11.1.4.meaning: Arwa': one whose bearing strikes awe.

12.1.4.meaning: Asbaha: woke to the morning. So the reciter, with three manuscripts cited by the editor al-Khatib and an old printing; the editions have sabbaha al-hayya, “raided the camp at dawn”.

15.1.5-6.head: بَنو مالِك
15.1.5-6.meaning: Banu Malik: a strong clan of Tayyi'. The amir raided them and took their herds and women; years later, the commentator says, drought and cold destroyed them, in 607 AH (1210–11 CE).

16.2.6.head: كاعِب
16.2.6.meaning: Ka'ib: a girl whose breasts have just grown, a young woman.

19.1.4.head: غَزِيَّة
19.1.4.meaning: Ghaziyya: a desert tribe, a branch of Tayyi' according to Ibn al-Kalbi and others; here the allies of al-Muntafiq.

24.1.4.head: فُواق
24.1.4.meaning: Fuwaq: the pause between two milkings of a camel; a moment.

25.2.4.head: التَّرائِب
25.2.4.meaning: Tara'ib: the upper breastbone, where a necklace hangs.

26.1.2-3.head: اِبن مَذكور
26.1.2-3.meaning: Ibn Madhkur: Nasir ibn Madhkur, chief of al-Muntafiq, a clan of Uqayl, who fled at the start of the fighting.

27.1.8.head: دَهمَش
27.1.8.meaning: Dahmash: Dahmash ibn Sanad ibn Ajwad, chief of Ghaziyya at the time.

28.2.4.head: الجَنيب
28.2.4.meaning: Janib: a spare horse led at a rider's side.

29.1.3-4.head: رَهط حُدَيثَة
29.1.3-4.meaning: The clan of Hudaytha: Mani' ibn Hudaytha and his kin.

29.2.2-3.head: جُرد الخَيل
29.2.2-3.meaning: Short-coated horses, a mark of good breeding.

31.2.2.head: عَبدَلِيّ
31.2.2.meaning: Abdali: of the line of Abd Allah ibn Ali. The editor al-Janbi takes him to be Abd Allah ibn Ali al-Shaykh, grandfather of the Uyunid founder of the same name and ancestor of both the amir and the poet.

32.2.2.meaning: Tawali: the hindmost riders in a chase.

33.1.5.head: جيرَة
33.1.5.meaning: Jira: protection, a grant of safe-conduct.

34.2.3.head: البَحرَين
34.2.3.meaning: Bahrain: in this period the whole Gulf coast of Arabia, al-Qatif, Awal and al-Ahsa, the Uyunid realm.

35.2.2-3.head: اِبن فَضل
35.2.2-3.meaning: Ibn Fadl: “son of Fadl”, the amir, after his forebear al-Fadl ibn Abd Allah.

36.1.1-2.head: فِتيان صِدق
36.1.1-2.meaning: “Young men of truth”: brave and loyal warriors.

36.1.4.head: عُقَيل
36.1.4.meaning: Uqayl: a tribe of Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, with clans in Iraq and Bahrain.

39.1.3-4.head: غُلب الرِّقاب
39.1.3-4.meaning: “The thick of neck”: the mighty and proud.

41.2.5.head: النَّوادِب
41.2.5.meaning: Nawadib: women who keen over the dead, listing their virtues.

42.1.4.head: عاد
42.1.4.meaning: Ad: an ancient Arab people, the people of the prophet Hud.

42.1.5.head: جُرهُم
42.1.5.meaning: Jurhum: an ancient Arab tribe that once held Mecca.

42.2.1-3.head: وُهَيب بن أَفصى
42.2.1-3.meaning: Wuhayb ibn Afsa: so the reciter, with two manuscripts cited and rejected by the editor al-Khatib. The editions have Hinb ibn Afsa, brother of Abd al-Qays, the forebear of the Uyunids, and ancestor of Bakr and Taghlib.

43.1.2-3.head: أَمير المُؤمِنين
43.1.2-3.meaning: Commander of the Faithful: the caliph's title; here the Abbasid al-Nasir li-Din Allah.

44.2.6.head: ناعِب
44.2.6.meaning: Na'ib: a tribe of Oman living on a mountain called Jabal al-Na'b, according to the commentator.

46.1.4.head: رَبيعَة
46.1.4.meaning: Rabi'a: Rabi'a ibn Nizar, the great tribal group to which Abd al-Qays and the Uyunids belong.
